title: Measuring angles by arc length
objectives: Define a radian as the angle whose arc equals the radius
Convert between degrees and radians in both directions
Use $s = r\theta$ and say why radians are the natural unit

screens.prose: A circle of radius $r$ has circumference $2\pi r$, where $\pi \approx 3.14159$. This circle has radius 1, so its whole circumference is $2\pi \approx 6.28$. The point has turned a quarter of the way round, and the arc it swept is shaded.
screens.question: How long is the shaded arc? Give two decimal places.

hints.text: What fraction of the whole circle is the arc?
The arc runs from the right-hand end of the horizontal axis to the top.
A quarter turn sweeps a quarter of the circumference: $6.28 \div 4$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the fraction of the turn, then that fraction of 6.28.

byKey.deg: 90 is the angle in degrees. The question asks for a length along the circle.
byKey.whole: That is the whole circumference. The point has gone only a quarter of the way round.
byKey.half: That is half the circumference, a half turn. A quarter turn is half of that again.
byKey.radius: The arc is longer than the radius. It curves round a quarter of the circle.
byKey.fraction: A quarter is the fraction of the turn. Now take a quarter of the circumference, 6.28.

explain.text: You took a quarter of the circumference: $2\pi \div 4 = \tfrac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.57$. On a circle of radius 1, every angle has an arc length like this. We will measure angles by it.

screens.prose: Move the slider to turn the point. The caption reads the length of the shaded arc as you go. The radius is 1.
screens.question: Slide until the arc is exactly as long as the radius, 1.00. Which angle is that closest to?

options.why: At 60° the straight chord equals the radius: that triangle is equilateral. The arc bulges outside the chord, so it is longer than 1.
At 45° the caption reads 0.79. The arc is still shorter than the radius.
At 90° the arc is 1.57, half as long again as the radius.

hints.text: Stop when the caption reads 1.00, then read the angle at the centre.

feedback.correct: An arc as long as the radius sits at about 57.3°.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide until the caption reads 1.00 and read the angle.

explain.text: At about 57.3° the arc is 1.00, the same as the radius. It is a little less than 60°, because the arc bulges outside the straight chord. This angle gets its own name next.

screens.prose: The angle whose arc equals the radius is **one radian**, about 57.3°. Measuring in **radians** means measuring an angle by its arc on a circle of radius 1. This point is at 1 radian.
screens.question: How many radians make a half turn?

options.why: 180 counts degrees. In radians we count arc lengths, and half the circumference is $\pi$.
That is the whole circumference, a full turn. A half turn sweeps half of it.
You halved one radian. A half turn is half of the circumference, not half of the radius.

hints.text: How long is the arc for a half turn?
A full turn sweeps the whole circumference, $2\pi$.
A half turn sweeps half of $2\pi$. That length is the angle in radians.

feedback.correct: A half turn sweeps an arc of $\pi$, so it is $\pi$ radians.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the arc length of a half turn on this circle.

explain.text: A half turn sweeps half the circumference: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 2\pi = \pi$. So $\pi$ radians is 180°. The angle's number is the arc's length.

screens.prose: The ticks mark the quarter turns. The point starts at 1 radian.
screens.question: Drag the point to $\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$ radians.

hints.text: $\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$ is three lots of $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$. How much of a turn is $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$?
$\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ is a quarter turn, from the right-hand end of the axis to the top.
Three quarter turns, anticlockwise from the right, end at the bottom of the circle.

feedback.correct: Three quarter turns: the bottom of the circle.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count quarter turns of $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ each.

byKey.quarter: You stopped at a quarter turn, $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ or about 1.57. We need three of those.
byKey.half: That is $\pi$, a half turn. $\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$ is a quarter turn further.
byKey.pt: The point is not at three quarter turns yet. The bottom of the circle is $\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$.

explain.text: Each quarter turn is $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, so three of them end at the bottom. That is $\tfrac{3\pi}{2} \approx 4.71$ radians, or 270°.

screens.prose: Now convert from degrees. A half turn is both 180° and $\pi$ radians.
screens.question: What is 45° in radians?

options.why: You divided 180 by 45, which turns the fraction upside down. 45° is a quarter of 180°, so it is a quarter of $\pi$.
You multiplied by $\pi$ but did not divide by 180. That is 45 half turns.
That is 90°, a quarter turn. 45° is half of that.

hints.text: What fraction of 180° is 45°?
45° is $\tfrac{45}{180} = \tfrac{1}{4}$ of a half turn. Take a quarter of $\pi$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find what fraction of 180° the angle is, then take that fraction of $\pi$.

explain.text: 45° is a quarter of 180°, so it is a quarter of $\pi$ radians. In one step: multiply by $\tfrac{\pi}{180}$. $45 \times \tfrac{\pi}{180} = \tfrac{\pi}{4} \approx 0.79$.

screens.prose: And back the other way. This point is at 2 radians, with no $\pi$ in sight.
screens.question: What is 2 radians in degrees? Give one decimal place.

hints.text: One radian is about 57.3°. How many radians are there here?
$\pi$ radians is 180°, so 1 radian is $\tfrac{180}{\pi}$ degrees.
Multiply 2 by $\tfrac{180}{\pi} \approx 57.296$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each radian is $\tfrac{180}{\pi}$ degrees.

byKey.wrong-way: You multiplied by $\tfrac{\pi}{180}$, the factor for degrees to radians. Going back, flip it: $\tfrac{180}{\pi}$.
byKey.two-pi: You read 2 as $2\pi$, a full turn. There is no $\pi$ here: it is 2 arc lengths of the radius.
byKey.sixty: You used 60° for a radian. A radian is a little less, about 57.3°.

explain.text: One radian is $\tfrac{180}{\pi} \approx 57.3^\circ$, so 2 radians is about 114.6°. The point sits in the second quadrant, just past the top. A number of radians without $\pi$ is still a fine angle.

screens.prose: Angles can go past a full turn. The point starts at 0, the right-hand end of the horizontal axis.
screens.question: The point turns $\tfrac{5\pi}{2}$ radians anticlockwise. Drag it to where it finishes.

hints.text: How many full turns of $2\pi$ fit inside $\tfrac{5\pi}{2}$?
$\tfrac{5\pi}{2} = 2\pi + \tfrac{\pi}{2}$.
One full turn brings the point back to the start. Then it goes a quarter turn more, to the top.

feedback.correct: One full turn, then a quarter turn: the top.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take away the full turns first.

byKey.start: You stopped after $2\pi$, one full turn. $\tfrac{5\pi}{2}$ goes a quarter turn further.
byKey.start2: You stopped after $2\pi$, one full turn. $\tfrac{5\pi}{2}$ goes a quarter turn further.
byKey.half: That is $\pi$, a half turn. Take away a full turn of $2\pi$ first: $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ is left.
byKey.pt: Not there yet. After one full turn, $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ is left to go.

explain.text: After $2\pi$ the point is back at the start: 0 and $2\pi$ are the same point. The remaining $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ takes it to the top. So $\tfrac{5\pi}{2}$ and $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ name the same point.

screens.prose: A colleague is asked to turn a point 6 radians. They know $\pi$ radians is 180°.
screens.question: How far round is 6 radians?

options.why: You treated each radian as 180°. That is $\pi$ radians, not one. 6 radians is $6 \times 57.3^\circ \approx 343.8^\circ$.
You read 6 radians as if it were 6°. A radian is about 57.3°, so 6 of them is almost a full turn.
A full turn is $2\pi \approx 6.28$ radians. 6 falls a little short of it.

options.text: Just short of one full turn

hints.text: How many radians is a full turn, as a decimal?
A full turn is $2\pi \approx 6.28$ radians. Compare 6 with 6.28.

feedback.correct: 6 is just less than $2\pi \approx 6.28$, so it is just short of a full turn.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare 6 with the number of radians in a full turn.

byKey.three-turns: You took a radian to be 180°. $\pi$ radians is 180°; one radian is only about 57.3°.

explain.text: A full turn is $2\pi \approx 6.28$ radians, so 6 radians stops 0.28 short. That is about 343.8°. The trap is reading “$\pi$ is 180°” as “a radian is 180°”.

screens.prose: A full turn is 360° and also $2\pi$ radians, the whole circumference. Halve both: $$\pi \text{ radians} = 180^\circ, \qquad \theta_{\text{rad}} = \theta_{\text{deg}} \times \frac{\pi}{180}.$$
screens.question: To turn an angle in radians into degrees, what do you multiply by?

options.why: That factor goes from degrees to radians. Going back, you undo it, so you flip it.
Multiplying by $\pi$ alone would make 1 radian about 3.14°. Each radian is about 57.3°.

hints.text: $\pi$ radians must come out as 180°.
What times $\pi$ gives 180? That number is $\tfrac{180}{\pi}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check your factor sends $\pi$ radians to 180°.

explain.text: You used $\tfrac{180}{\pi}$ to turn 2 radians into 114.6°. It sends $\pi$ to 180, as it must. The two factors undo each other.

screens.prose: Radians made arc length easy on a circle of radius 1. Now take any radius $r$ and an angle $\theta$ in radians.
screens.question: Put the lines in order to find the arc length $s$.

lines.text: A full turn sweeps the whole circumference, $2\pi r$
A full turn is $2\pi$ radians, so $\theta$ is the fraction $\dfrac{\theta}{2\pi}$ of a turn
$s = \dfrac{\theta}{2\pi} \times 2\pi r$, the same fraction of the circumference

hints.text: Begin with the length of the whole circle.
Next say what fraction of a full turn $\theta$ is.
Circumference, then the fraction, then the fraction of the circumference, then cancel.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the full circumference, then take a fraction of it.

byKey.d4: Cancelling comes after you have written $s$ as a fraction of the circumference.
byKey.d3: You need the fraction $\tfrac{\theta}{2\pi}$ before you can take it of the circumference.

explain.text: The $2\pi$ cancels and leaves $s = r\theta$. In degrees the same arc is $s = \tfrac{\pi r \theta}{180}$, with a factor stuck on. Radians remove that factor, which is why they are the natural unit.

screens.prose: A retailer's sales follow a yearly cycle. An analyst models the cycle as a point going once round a circle every 12 months. Each month the point turns the same angle.

state.caption: One month of the cycle: the ticks mark the 12 months

screens.question: How many radians does the point turn each month? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: How many radians is the whole cycle?
The whole year is one full turn, $2\pi$ radians.
Share $2\pi$ equally over 12 months.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide one full turn, in radians, by 12.

byKey.degrees: 30 is the angle in degrees. The model works in radians, so use $2\pi$ for the full turn.
byKey.turns: That is the fraction of a turn per month. Multiply it by $2\pi$ to get radians.
byKey.times: You multiplied $2\pi$ by 12. The year shares one turn over 12 months, so divide.

explain.text: A full cycle is $2\pi$ radians, so each month turns $\tfrac{\pi}{6} \approx 0.5236$. This rate is the cycle's **angular frequency**, written $\omega$. Models of cycles use it in radians, so that no factor of $\tfrac{\pi}{180}$ appears.

ideas: One radian is the angle whose arc is as long as the radius, about 57.3°.
A full turn is $2\pi$ radians and a half turn is $\pi$, so 0 and $2\pi$ are the same point.
With $\theta$ in radians the arc is $s = r\theta$, with no conversion factor: that is why radians are natural.

formula.name: Degrees and radians
formula.note: Multiply by $\tfrac{\pi}{180}$ to reach radians, and by $\tfrac{180}{\pi}$ to come back.

summary.trap: A radian is not 180°. $\pi$ radians is 180°; one radian is about 57.3°, so 6 radians is just short of a full turn.

options.why: You turned the fraction $\tfrac{150}{180}$ upside down. 150° is less than a half turn, so it is less than $\pi$.
You multiplied by $\pi$ without dividing by 180.
That is 300°. You divided by 90 instead of 180.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply by $\tfrac{\pi}{180}$ and simplify.

explain.text: $\tfrac{150}{180} = \tfrac{5}{6}$, so 150° is $\tfrac{5}{6}$ of a half turn. That is $\tfrac{5\pi}{6}$ radians.

quiz.question: What is 3 radians in degrees? Give one decimal place.

byKey.wrong-way: You multiplied by $\tfrac{\pi}{180}$. That factor goes the other way.
byKey.pi-180: You treated each radian as 180°. Only $\pi$ radians make 180°.

explain.text: Each radian is $\tfrac{180}{\pi} \approx 57.3^\circ$. Three of them make about 171.9°, just short of a half turn. That fits: 3 is just less than $\pi$.

quiz.prose: A circle has radius 2. An angle of $\tfrac{\pi}{3}$ radians sits at its centre.
quiz.question: How long is the arc? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $s = r\theta$ with $\theta$ in radians.

byKey.degrees: You used 60°, the angle in degrees. $s = r\theta$ needs $\theta$ in radians.
byKey.no-r: That is the arc on a circle of radius 1. This radius is 2, so the arc is twice as long.

explain.text: With $\theta$ in radians, $s = r\theta = 2 \times \tfrac{\pi}{3} = \tfrac{2\pi}{3} \approx 2.09$. Doubling the radius doubled the arc.

quiz.prose: Angles are measured anticlockwise from the right-hand end of the horizontal axis.
quiz.question: Which angle names the same point as 0?

options.why: That is a half turn, to the opposite side of the circle.
360 counts degrees. 360 radians is about 57.3 turns, which does not land back on 0.
1 radian is about 57.3°, part way into the first quadrant.

feedback.correct: A full turn of $2\pi$ brings the point back to 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which angle is exactly one full turn?

explain.text: One full turn is $2\pi$ radians, and it ends where it began. So 0 and $2\pi$ are the same point. 360 radians is not a whole number of turns.
